MHD-INT es un simulador que modela la ev: MHD-INT is a simulator that models the time evolution of planets and young stars, calculating how their magnetic field, orbit, rotation and atmosphere change over millions or billions of years. It lets you answer questions such as "why is Earth habitable and Mars not?" or "what would happen if Earth had a bigger moon?".
Gravedad y órbitas: las leyes de Kepler: Gravity and orbits: Kepler's and Newton's laws
Todo lo que orbita algo más masivo (un p: Anything that orbits something more massive (a planet around its star, a moon around its planet) follows, to a good approximation, an ellipse — not a perfect circle. Kepler discovered this by observing real data of Mars (early 17th century); Newton explained *why* a century later: the gravitational force between two bodies is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them (F = G·M·m/r²). From this comes Kepler's Third Law, which MHD-INT uses constantly: the square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of the orbit (P² ∝ a³), and it depends on the star's mass. It is the same equation the Ephemerides, N-body and Resonances modules use to compute orbital periods.
Estrellas: qué son y cómo cambian con el: Stars: what they are and how they change over time
Una estrella es una esfera de gas (sobre: A star is a sphere of gas (mostly hydrogen) massive enough for gravity to compress its core until nuclear fusion ignites, releasing the energy we see as light. Stars are not static: they are born surrounded by a disk of gas and dust (the protoplanetary disk, where planets form), they spin fast when young and slow down with age as the stellar wind carries away angular momentum (a process called magnetic braking). They also emit more high-energy radiation (X-rays, ultraviolet) when young, which matters a lot for the atmospheres of planets orbiting closely. MHD-INT models this stellar evolution (rotation, wind, luminosity) to know how the conditions a planet receives change throughout its life, not just today.
Los planetas se forman dentro del disco: Planets form inside the protoplanetary disk surrounding a young star: dust particles collide and stick together, forming ever larger bodies (from dust to pebble, from pebble to planetesimal, from planetesimal to planet), in a process that takes a few million years. The place where a planet forms is not necessarily where it ends up: planets can *migrate*, changing their distance from the star through gravitational interaction with the disk gas (this is what MHD-INT's Migration module models). When several planets migrate at related speeds, they can become trapped in an orbital resonance — their orbital periods end up in a ratio of small whole numbers (see below). MHD-INT does not simulate the formation of planets themselves (the accretion from dust to planet), but it does simulate their later evolution: migration, resonances and internal physics once the planet already exists.
Un planeta con un núcleo de metal líquid: A planet with a liquid-metal core in convective motion (like Earth's molten-iron outer core) can generate its own magnetic field through a mechanism called a dynamo: the motion of an electrically conductive fluid, combined with the planet's rotation, twists the magnetic field lines and amplifies them, much like a bicycle dynamo converts motion into electricity. This magnetic field deflects the stellar wind (charged particles the star constantly emits) before it reaches the planet's atmosphere, forming a protected bubble called the magnetosphere. Without that shield, the stellar wind can erode the atmosphere over time — this is believed to be part of what happened to Mars. This is the physical heart of MHD-INT: calculating whether a planet generates enough field, and whether that field is enough to protect its atmosphere, throughout its entire history.
La zona habitable, y por qué no alcanza: The habitable zone, and why it is not enough
La \"zona habitable\" clásica es el rang: The classical "habitable zone" is the range of distances from a star where liquid water could exist on a planet's surface, depending on how much light it receives. It is a useful but incomplete concept: a planet can be in the radiative habitable zone and still not be habitable, if it lost its atmosphere for lack of a magnetic shield (as possibly happened to Mars) or if its orbit is so eccentric that the climate varies too much. MHD-INT does not replace the radiative habitable-zone calculation (that depends on the star's luminosity, which it does use as an input), but it adds a layer that almost no publicly available simulator models: whether the planet keeps its magnetic shield and its atmosphere over billions of years. That is why the project's central result is called the *Magnetic* Habitability Index (MHI), not simply "habitability": it measures one additional necessary condition, not the whole story.

⚠️ Hay una quinta pieza, la penalización: ⚠️ There is a fifth piece, the extreme-obliquity penalty (-20 points if ε > 60°), but it **only applies to 5 bodies with measured real obliquity**: Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Uranus and Venus. For the rest of the database (almost all exoplanets), obliquity is an unknown value, not a low one — penalizing an unmeasured value would introduce a bias with no physical basis. If you simulate an exoplanet and do not see this penalty acting, that is expected, not a bug.
Cuando hay más de dos cuerpos gravitando: When more than two bodies gravitate toward each other (a star and several planets, for example), there is no closed formula like Kepler's ellipses — you have to compute the gravitational force of each body on all the others and integrate the motion step by step in time. This is the "N-body problem". MHD-INT uses a symplectic integrator (velocity Verlet), chosen because it conserves the system's energy and angular momentum very well over long integrations, something simpler integrators do not guarantee.

Dos planetas están en resonancia orbital: Two planets are in orbital resonance when their periods keep a ratio of small whole numbers (2:1, 3:2, 5:2...). It is no coincidence: it is usually the result of planetary migration — as planets move closer to or farther from their star, their periods change, and if at some point they fall into a simple ratio, the resonance itself "traps" them and stabilizes that relationship.

Módulo 🌀 Migración y Resonancias (resona: Module 🌀 Migration and Resonances (resonancias.py). It detects kinematic resonant candidates (from the periods, not from a long dynamical integration confirming the capture). Validated with two real, well-documented cases in the literature: the 5:2 resonance between Jupiter and Saturn (the "Great Inequality") and the 7-planet resonant chain of TRAPPIST-1 (Agol et al. 2021).
Una \"alineación planetaria\" en el sent: A "planetary alignment" in the sense the media report it is a perspective phenomenon: several planets appear grouped in a small region of the sky as seen from Earth, even though in real space they are at enormous distances from each other and do not form any physical line. It is apparent geometry, not a physical alignment. The combined gravitational effect of such an alignment on Earth is negligible compared with that of the Moon — tidal force falls off with the cube of the distance, and the planets are too far away to compete with a body as close as the Moon, no matter how many line up.
Módulo 🪐 Catálogo de Sistemas (detector_: Module 🪐 System Catalog (detector_alineacion.py): it computes the apparent ecliptic longitude of each planet as seen from Earth and finds the instant of smallest angular dispersion among them. It is explicitly documented that this measures geometry, not tidal force — MHD-INT does not model planet-planet gravity on Earth in any module, on purpose.
Venus rota al revés que casi todos los d: Venus rotates backwards compared with almost all the other planets of the Solar System, and very slowly (a Venusian day lasts longer than its year). One of the hypotheses to explain it is the atmospheric thermal tide: solar heating of Venus's extremely dense atmosphere generates a tidal pattern in the air that exerts a net torque on the solid planet, able to slow it and even reverse its rotation over billions of years — unlike the solid gravitational tide, which on its own would tend to slow it but not to reverse it.
Fase 1 del motor (engine.py, flag torque: Engine Phase 1 (engine.py, flag torque_atmosferico_on, disabled by default). With the flag on, Venus does end up in retrograde rotation in the simulation — with a ~26% error against the observed value, documented as pending fine calibration, not as a final result.
Una efeméride es la posición y velocidad: An ephemeris is the real, measured position and velocity of a Solar System body on a specific date — it is observational data, not the result of any simulation. It differs from "simulating from year 0" in that it starts from where the body *really is today*, instead of an arbitrary or hypothetical initial position.
Módulo 🛰️ Efemérides reales, que consult: Module 🛰️ Real Ephemerides, which queries JPL Horizons (NASA/JPL) directly. Also used as an optional initial condition in the System Catalog (n_cuerpos_real.py) so that an N-body simulation starts from the real configuration of the Solar System on a chosen date, instead of arbitrary phases — only available for the Solar System, because Horizons does not cover exoplanets.
Cuando una estrella joven tiene un campo: When a young star has a strong magnetic field, that field can "cut" the gas disk surrounding it before it reaches the stellar surface, creating an inner gap (the truncation radius). The magnetic interaction between the star and the disk can also gradually misalign the star's rotation axis relative to the disk plane over time, depending on how strong the coupling is compared with the star's inertia.
Módulo 🌌 Disco Protoplanetario (Beta), b: Module 🌌 Protoplanetary Disk (Beta), based on Lai, Foucart & Lin (2011). It validates the bi-stable alignment/misalignment regime according to the ζ̃/λ ratio, and the truncation radius against the real case of the T Tauri star DO Tau (Bessolaz et al. 2008), with a documented error of ~13-15%.
MHD-INT combina dos fuerzas en cada simu: MHD-INT combines two forces in every simulation: gravity, which governs orbital motion, and magnetism, which governs the planet's protection. They are not independent: they form a cycle.
gravedad → determina la órbita (distanci: gravity → determines the orbit (distance to the star) → the distance determines how much stellar wind the planet receives (1/distance² factor, closer = more wind) → the wind compresses the magnetosphere → the magnetic field (if strong enough) protects the atmosphere → the atmosphere takes part in the torque that slows or reverses the rotation (the Venus case) → the rotation feeds the dynamo that generates the magnetic field, closing the cycle.

2. Calcular la presión de viento (P_ram): 2. Compute the wind pressure (P_ram) the planet receives, already scaled by its real distance from the star.
3. Calcular el torque magnético, el núme: 3. Compute the magnetic torque, the Elsasser number (how vigorous the dynamo is) and the magnetosphere radius, with an ohmic correction that depends on that same Elsasser number.
4. Calcular el calor de marea total (por: 4. Compute the total tidal heat (from eccentricity, plus the extra contribution from obliquity if the planet has a significant one).

That is why Venus is excluded from the rotation-direction check in Validation mode.
10. Sumar solo los torques cuyo interrup: 10. Add up only the torques whose switch is on, and update the rotation speed.
11. Actualizar la órbita (semieje y exce: 11. Update the orbit (semi-major axis and eccentricity) with the changes computed in step 5.
12. Actualizar el campo magnético: si el: 12. Update the magnetic field: if the thermal model is on, a real dynamo (it regenerates if the magnetic Reynolds number exceeds 40, otherwise it decays); if not, a simplified decay that slows down according to the Elsasser number.

MHD-INT no calcula fuerza de marea entre: MHD-INT does not compute tidal force between planets -- on purpose, it does not model planet-planet gravity on Earth in any module (see Theoretical Framework, topic 'Planetary alignments'). This is a manual-calculation exercise with the tidal formula (F_tide ∝ M/d³) and real mass/distance data, designed so that the numerical result reinforces why an apparent alignment is not a physically relevant event for Earth.

Alineaciones Aparentes y el MHI: ¿Están: Apparent Alignments and the MHI: Are They Coupled?
¿Una alineación planetaria aparente coin: Does an apparent planetary alignment coincide with any detectable change in Earth's MHI on that same date?
El detector de alineación (Catálogo de S: The alignment detector (System Catalog) and the MHI calculation (main engine, engine.py/habitabilidad.py) are two completely independent simulation systems that share no state: one integrates the orbital positions of several bodies (N-body), the other evolves the magnetic field/atmosphere of ONE isolated planet. There is no expected physical mechanism connecting them -- in fact, that is the exercise's pedagogical conclusion: an apparent alignment does not have to affect (and does not affect) a planet's magnetic shield. A good question to discuss why they should NOT be coupled, not an experiment the software can run.
¿Puede el campo magnético de un planeta: Can the magnetic field of an active planet influence that of an inactive neighboring planet?
MHD-INT no modela ningún tipo de interac: MHD-INT does not model any kind of magnetic interaction between planets -- neither the main engine (which simulates each planet in isolation) nor the N-body module (which only integrates gravity, without magnetic fields). Physically, moreover, the distance between planets makes any direct magnetic coupling negligible compared with each planet's interaction with the wind and field of its own star. A legitimate research question in other contexts (e.g. very close Jupiter moons), but outside this software's current scope.

Nuestra estrella, fotografiada en luz ul: Our star, photographed in extreme ultraviolet light by the Solar Dynamics Observatory. What you see is not the visible surface but the corona, the Sun's outer atmosphere, heated to millions of degrees by magnetic processes that are still not fully understood. The solar wind (the one MHD-INT models with real NOAA data) comes precisely from this region.
NASA/SDO (Solar Dynamics Observatory), v: NASA/SDO (Solar Dynamics Observatory), via Wikimedia Commons -- featured image
El planeta más cercano al Sol y el más p: The planet closest to the Sun and the smallest in the Solar System. Despite its size, it has a weak but real global magnetic field -- something that surprised scientists, because such a small core was expected to have cooled and solidified long ago. It has practically no atmosphere to protect.
Venus está permanentemente cubierto de n: Venus is permanently covered in clouds of sulfuric acid -- this image is a radar mosaic, not visible light, because that is the only way to see its real surface. It spins backwards compared with almost all other planets, and very slowly: a Venusian day lasts longer than its year.
NASA/JPL (mosaico radar Magellan + Pione: NASA/JPL (radar mosaic Magellan + Pioneer Venus + Venera 13/14), via Wikimedia Commons -- featured image
La icónica \"Canica Azul\", tomada por l: The iconic "Blue Marble", taken by the Apollo 17 crew on their way to the Moon -- one of the most reproduced photographs in history. The magnetic field generated by Earth's liquid iron core deflects the solar wind and protects the atmosphere that makes life on the surface possible.
El único satélite natural de la Tierra,: Earth's only natural satellite, probably formed about 4.5 billion years ago by the impact of a Mars-sized body on the newly formed Earth. The Moon stabilizes the tilt of Earth's axis (the obliquity) over the long term -- without it, Earth's climate would be far more chaotic.
El \"planeta rojo\", fotografiado por el: The "red planet", photographed by Hubble during one of its close approaches to Earth. Mars once had a global magnetic field -- fossil magnetism can still be detected in its crust -- but its dynamo shut down billions of years ago, and with it went a good part of its atmosphere.
NASA/ESA, Telescopio Espacial Hubble, ví: NASA/ESA, Hubble Space Telescope, via Wikimedia Commons
El planeta más grande del Sistema Solar,: The largest planet in the Solar System, with the strongest magnetic field of all the planets -- generated by a core of metallic hydrogen, not liquid iron as on Earth. Its gravity dominates the dynamics of the entire outer solar system, including the orbits of asteroids and comets.
Fotografiado por la sonda Cassini durant: Photographed by the Cassini probe during Saturn's equinox, when grazing light makes subtle details in the rings visible. Saturn is so low in density that, if a bathtub large enough existed, it would float on water.
NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute (misión: NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute (Cassini mission), via Wikimedia Commons
Urano gira prácticamente \"de costado\":: Uranus rotates practically "on its side": its rotation axis is tilted about 98°, almost parallel to the plane of its orbit -- the most extreme obliquity of any planet in the Solar System, probably due to an ancient collision. It is the only planet that MHD-INT flags with that extreme-obliquity penalty.
El planeta más lejano del Sistema Solar,: The farthest planet in the Solar System, and the only one discovered by mathematical prediction before direct observation -- astronomers noticed that something was perturbing the orbit of Uranus, calculated where that something should be, and found it there. It has the fastest winds measured on any planet.
Nuestra propia galaxia, vista desde dent: Our own galaxy, seen from the inside -- which is why we see it as a band of diffuse light crossing the night sky, not as the full spiral disk that would be visible from outside. The Sun and the entire Solar System orbit the galactic center, completing one revolution every ~225 million years.
La galaxia espiral grande más cercana a: The large spiral galaxy closest to the Milky Way, about 2.5 million light-years away -- close enough to be seen with the naked eye on a dark night. Andromeda and the Milky Way are approaching each other through mutual gravity and are expected to collide (and merge) in several billion years.
